hits.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015). hits.text: Introduction Mental health disorders typically emerge in early adulthood (De Lijster et al., 2016) and rates can be especially high in college students (Eisenberg et al., 2013). A survey of 571 college campus counseling centers found that anxiety was the number one reason that students sought counseling (LiViness et al., 2017). Anxiety disorders are the most common mental health conditions reported among college students at 11.9% (Pedrelli et. al, 2015). Many college students likely experience inflated rates of anxiety, related to multiple aspects of collegiate life, such as increased responsibility, financial concerns, academic performance, and acceptance to graduate programs, with rates of anxiety and other disorders (e.g., depression) varying across discipline and class rank (Bieter et al., 2015; Lipson et al., 2016). Identifying students’ mental health disorders can result in earlier intervention and improve their chances of degree completion (Hunt et al., 2010). For students with anxiety, using a self-report questionnaire may be the first step in identifying a problem and encouraging them to seek treatment. Self-report questionnaires allow for both professionals and nonprofessionals to identify a probable disorder and assess the severity of symptoms. Ideally, such questionnaires are brief, accurate, and easy to administer. Many are available online and can be done quickly, privately, and remotely. The GAD-7 is a seven-item questionnaire used as a screening tool for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and as a measure for anxiety symptom severity. Creating successful preventative and intervention plans requires an understanding of the many, multi-level factors that contribute to psychological discomfort. The objective of this scoping review was to use the Socio-Ecological Model (SEM) to map the determinants of psychological distress among college students in a comprehensive manner. Methods: A total of 15 review publi- cations published between 2015 and 2024, including narrative reviews, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and umbrella reviews, were analyzed under the guidance of PRISMA ScR. These studies synthesized evidence across various countries, including China, Iran, India, Canada, Egypt, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, and the United States. Results: Academic pressure, financial stress, poor sleep, unhealthy coping mechanisms, and pre-existing mental health issues were all individual-level concerns, with female and minority students being more vulnerable. Strong familial ties and friendships served as protective interpersonal support. Heavy academic workloads, strict grading guidelines, a lack of mental health resources, and unwelcoming campus environments were among the institutional factors. Stigma and socioeconomic disparities are examples of community-level variables that make mental health issues worse. Conclusions: Student mental health is shaped by interrelated factors across all SEM levels. Integrated, multi-level strategies are essential to fostering supportive campuses, strengthening community networks, and implementing inclusive policies that promote mental health equity. Available Knowledge/Review of the Literature According to the U.S. Preventative Services Task Force (USPSTF), depression is among the leading causes of disability in individuals 15 years of age and older (Siu & U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), 2016). By 2020, depressive disorders are predicted to be the second leading cause of disability and death (Soltani, Smith, Beck, & Johnson, 2014). Prevalence of depression among college students accounts for approximately 16.7% and is more than twice as common among college students compared to the general population (Liu et al., 2019; English & Campbell, 2019). Thus, depression is highly prevalent and appears to be increasing. Depression is one of the leading health concerns in college population, yet roughly half of college students with depression receive treatment (English & Campbell, 2019). Mental health among college students affects important outcomes such as social connectedness, academic performance, academic retention, and future economic productivity, which should be a significant concern for certain stakeholders such as campus administrators, college professors, and parents (Lipson, Gaddis, Heinze, & Eisenberg, 2015; Ebert et al., 2018). In addition, depression has been associated with increased health care costs such as emergency department visits and inpatient hospitalizations (Wright et al., 2015).
